records.title: Language requirements in hospital information systems
records.subtitle: How healthcare digital transformation creates demand for multilingual patient engagement and language technology
records.display_title: Language requirements in hospital information systems: How healthcare digital transformation creates demand for multilingual patient engagement and language technology
records.abstract: Hospital information systems are becoming the foundation of digital healthcare, extending patient interactions across telehealth, remote monitoring, self-service platforms, and AI-enabled services. This report examines how these changes create growing requirements for translation, localization, interpreting, cultural adaptation, and multilingual AI governance. It explains why language access has become a strategic capability that affects patient safety, digital adoption, regulatory compliance, and health outcomes, and provides practical recommendations for healthcare organizations, language service providers, and technology vendors seeking to build multilingual healthcare technologies by design.

records.title: Smartling centers quality governance in the post-TMS platform
records.subtitle: Vendor Briefing
records.display_title: Smartling centers quality governance in the post-TMS platform: Vendor Briefing
records.abstract: As AI-enabled translation becomes increasingly commoditized, enterprise attention is shifting from away translation generation to quality governance, explainability, and risk management. Using Smartling’s latest platform direction as a lens, this briefing examines how the post-TMS market is evolving from translation management to multilingual content governance. It analyzes what Smartling’s approach reveals about the future of enterprise language platforms, where vendors are likely to differentiate, and which capabilities organizations should prioritize as they evaluate technology investments. Enterprise localization, globalization, content, and AI leaders, along with technology buyers, will gain practical insights to inform platform strategy and prepare for the next generation of multilingual content management.

records.subtitle: A system-level localization and globalization maturity framework
records.display_title: LMM 4.0: Enterprise global content maturity model: A system-level localization and globalization maturity framework
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Alison Toon, Dr. Arle Lommel, Peter Coleman
records.abstract: Organizations face growing pressure to manage continuous content creation, global distribution, AI-enabled workflows, and increasingly complex multilingual operations. This report introduces the Localization Maturity Model (LMM) 4.0, an enterprise capability maturity framework. LMM 4.0 extends and unifies CSA Research's earlier localization and globalization maturity models into a single system spanning people, processes, technology, governance, and data. It provides a structured approach to assessing and improving global content capabilities, enabling organizations to benchmark current maturity, identify gaps, prioritize investments, and build the operational capability required to scale global content effectively. You can’t manage what you don’t measure. For executive management, strategists, and departmental or sector leaders, LMM 4.0 provides a way to address this challenge across global content operations.

records.title: Human at the Core, AI in the Loop
records.subtitle: How artificial intelligence can augment human expertise to drive scale and quality
records.display_title: Human at the Core, AI in the Loop: How artificial intelligence can augment human expertise to drive scale and quality
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping multilingual communication, but the central question is no longer whether AI will participate: it already does. The challenge is determining where expertise, judgment, governance, and accountability should reside. This report presents CSA Research’s vision of “Human at the Core, AI in the Loop,” arguing that AI should augment and extend human capability rather than replace it, with professionals defining objectives, exercising judgment, and remaining accountable while AI supports those goals. The report explores what this shift means for language and global content providers, enterprise buyers, technology developers, and professional linguists, and provides a practical framework for designing workflows and strategies that combine AI scale with human expertise to deliver outcomes that machines alone cannot achieve.

records.title: Technical and pricing changes in LLMs challenge language sector business models
records.display_title: Technical and pricing changes in LLMs challenge language sector business models
records.abstract: As organizations across the language sector build products, workflows, and services around large language models (LLMs), many assume that AI costs will continue to decline. This report examines how technical changes, shifting pricing models, and evolving deployment architectures are instead quietly increasing the true cost of AI. Rising token consumption and cost, the move from fine-tuning to RAG, and the end of unlimited API access are reshaping the economics of AI adoption. The findings have significant implications for budgeting, pricing, vendor strategy, and risk management. Executives, product leaders, localization professionals, and AI strategists can use this report to assess their exposure, strengthen planning, and prepare for a future in which AI costs are higher, less predictable, and strategically consequential.

CSA Research finds that this model could reduce operational complexity, improve governance, and support more scalable AI-enabled content strategies. The report explores what this emerging post-TMS approach means for enterprises, global content solutions companies, and technology leaders seeking greater control, efficiency, and flexibility in global content operations.

records.abstract: Enterprises are rethinking translation management as automation options, including AI and GenAI, offer opportunities beyond traditional translation management systems (TMSes), raising the question of whether to build, buy, or combine approaches. This research shows that custom environments can introduce complexity and hidden costs, while commercial systems remain stronger for scale and governance, leading most organizations toward hybrid models. For most but not all organizations, this indicates a shift toward integrated ecosystems rather than full replacement strategies. This matters because translation infrastructure directly affects cost, risk, and global performance. Enterprise buyers and language service providers can use this report to guide strategy and investment decisions.

records.display_title: The K-shaped language sector
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: For much of the past decade, the language services and solutions industry was known for its resilience. Even when the broader economy softened, the sector often continued to expand as enterprises pushed into new markets, digital products proliferated, and content volumes grew. That pattern has changed. Since 2019, growth has slowed and, in inflation-adjusted terms, the market has trended downward. This brief helps explain both why some providers report accelerating declines while others see relative stability, and why the future of the sector will be defined less by “more translation” and more by what comes next.

records.title: How regulated localization differs from High-Tech
records.subtitle: 22 major differences in language needs and practices
records.display_title: How regulated localization differs from High-Tech: 22 major differences in language needs and practices
records.abstract: Although high-tech fields are moving rapidly toward AI-first approaches to language management, regulated industries are not. Organizations in highly regulated sectors still require extensive human involvement to meet strict compliance standards. Errors can lead to financial penalties, health risks, or even loss of life. Localization professionals transitioning from AI-first environments into regulated organizations may experience significant cultural shifts, along with pressure to introduce AI and automation safely. Language service and technology providers are also exploring opportunities in this space. But is this a strategic opportunity, or a market that demands experience and specialized expertise?

records.subtitle: From operational output to strategic enterprise asset
records.display_title: The transformational imperative: Reframing global content: From operational output to strategic enterprise asset
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Dr. Arle Lommel, Alison Toon, Fatima Bengana
records.abstract: As the language industry moves further into its post-localization phase, it faces fundamental structural changes: Global content is no longer a translation problem – it’s an enterprise transformation challenge. This report explains where transformation pressure originates, how it multiplies across channels and markets, and what enterprises and providers must build to keep pace. In this deep examination, CSA Research maps the next phase of demand for multilingual, multimodal content transformation – driven by AI, metadata, personalization, and the dispersion of content from enterprise cores to the edge. Enterprises and service providers alike will find a clear framework for understanding what must be transformed, where content lives, and why the opportunity extends well beyond translation into enterprise-wide content operations.

While near-term conditions remain challenging, the findings point to emerging opportunities for organizations that pivot toward value-driven global content solutions, redefining the role of human expertise in an AI-augmented future.

records.title: Metrix 2.0™ origins and purpose
records.subtitle: Quick Take
records.display_title: Metrix 2.0™ origins and purpose: Quick Take
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: This report explains the rationale behind CSA Research’s updated capability maturity model for global content solutions providers (GCSPs). Building on our long history with frameworks such as the LSP Metrix™, the Globalization Maturity Model™ the Localization Maturity Model™, we trace the emergence of GCSPs and the shift from “language services” to “content solutions.” We detail how we constructed Metrix 2.0™ by combining Carnegie Mellon’s capability maturity model (CMM) foundations with 25 years of research, consulting engagements, and industry input. The result is a practical, research-driven framework that supports global enterprises, solutions providers, and investors in: 1) benchmarking provider maturity, 2) understanding evolving roles in the post-localization era, and 3) identifying the pathways required for providers to successfully compete in a content-driven global economy.

records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: This report updates the original LSP Metrix capability maturity model to reflect the realities of the post-localization era. As language services evolve into global content solutions, this framework charts six progressive stages, ranging from traditional LSPs to fully realized Global Content Solutions Providers (GCSPs). It addresses the disruptive influence of AI, automation, and data-driven workflows, while highlighting the growing demand for speed, scalability, and strategic alignment with enterprise digital initiatives. By defining new dimensions of performance and specialization, Metrix 2.0 offers providers, buyers, and investors a roadmap to assess capabilities, benchmark progress, and plan transformation in a global market where content is now a core business asset

records.title: Labs: The enabler for global content solutions
records.display_title: Labs: The enabler for global content solutions

records.abstract: A Lab that enables LSPs to provide customized solutions is an essential engine that enables them to drive their shift from transactional services to solution-driven partnerships that deliver measurable ROI and lasting differentiation. It signals the provider’s technology vision and readiness to meet enterprise requirements for AI readiness, innovation capacity, and fluency in real-world use cases. The Lab is a vital asset as they progress along the path defined in Metrix 2.0 toward becoming Global Content Solutions Providers (GCSPs). The form the Lab takes depends on where the LSPs are on that journey, their size, and their strategy, but it provides independence and capability to chart their own course and to be seen as more than providers of words.

Its performance in this trial is telling because evaluating translation requires comparing source and target texts, understanding the correlations between the two, and making value judgments about the choices that translators must make.

records.title: Why terminologists are essential for reliable knowledge graphs
records.display_title: Why terminologists are essential for reliable knowledge graphs
records.abstract: Our recent reports on knowledge graphs (“Taming Global Content with Knowledge Graphs” and “Fundamentals of Multilingual Knowledge Graphs”) focused on the ways that they help enterprises solve basic problems in search and information discovery, compliance, customer care, and other enterprise functions. In this report, we address how and why terminologists should play a critical role in building these resources by ensuring that they work across languages and interoperate with terminology databases. Terminologists bring a skill set that accelerates this work while connecting it to existing content initiatives. However, it requires them to understand the tools, technologies, and standards behind knowledge graphs before they can apply their expertise. This report discusses the role they play and how they can get involved in improving knowledge management.

records.title: TransPerfect’s GlobalLink reimagines pricing
records.subtitle: Vendor Briefing
records.display_title: TransPerfect’s GlobalLink reimagines pricing: Vendor Briefing
records.abstract: The struggle for a new and realistic industry pricing model is real: the mix of human, MT, and AI naturally flows towards effort-based reimbursement. However, while enterprises and LSPs often talk about simplifying the way they pay for language services, most will challenge any new pricing structure that does not allow them to easily predict, measure, and budget for costs. An optional process within TransPerfect’s GlobalLink TMS challenges these traditional pricing structures. It measures actual effort to set pricing on the true work needed to deliver the required quality. This vendor briefing examines the technology, its potential, and its opportunity to make a real change in translation pricing.

records.title: Fundamentals of multilingual knowledge graphs
records.display_title: Fundamentals of multilingual knowledge graphs
records.abstract: Knowledge graphs are an emerging tool for representing organizational knowledge in machine-processible form. They link entities – such as products, components, people, or processes – and properties into a network of relations. They allow algorithms to operate based on knowledge about these entities rather than superficial searches based on strings. A companion to the more technically oriented “Taming Global Content with Knowledge Graphs,” this visual report provides an executive-friendly overview of knowledge graphs, their benefits, and how these systems function – with an emphasis on multilingual requirements.

records.abstract: On February 27, Inception Labs released Mercury Coder, a new type of large language model (LLM). It uses so-called “diffusion model” approaches pioneered for image generation to create text responses all at once, rather than token by token, as is currently done with ChatGPT, Gemini, and other GenAI platforms. The big difference this approach makes is in speed, with Ars Technica reporting that coding tasks are 5.5 to 19 times faster than current top LLMs. Mercury Coder is optimized for software code, but it will perform other tasks. Here’s what we found when we tested it for translation.

records.title: Is DeepSeek a game changer for translation?
records.subtitle: Ask the Analyst
records.display_title: Is DeepSeek a game changer for translation?: Ask the Analyst
records.abstract: The public release in January 2025 of DeepSeek’s V3 large language model (LLM) – accessible via a ChatGPT-like user interface – prompted an existential crisis in the AI developer community. Early reports claimed that it had been produced for just US$5 million but performed roughly on par with OpenAI’s GPT-4. Even though later coverage said that the actual costs were much higher, stock prices for leading AI companies dropped substantially after DeepSeek was released, although they later rebounded. Aside from DeepSeek’s broader long-term consequences, many of our clients asked for our take on V3’s translation capabilities. They wanted to know if it offers any advantages beyond price. records.abstract: Automated quality estimation (AQE) and automated post-editing (APE) are techniques to reduce the amount of human activity needed to check or improve the output of translation, typically machine translation. records.subtitle: From our blog

records.abstract: In October 2023, we argued that the future of AI would be in “focused large language models” (FLLMs). These are purpose-built language models that target a specific industry, set of languages, or task and that are correspondingly smaller than the large language models (LLMs) being created by OpenAI, Google, Meta, and others. Those massive models – GPT-4o has over 175 billion parameters – are like Swiss Army knives: They are prepared to handle almost any task, from creating a haiku to drawing pictures of cats. How well they do these tasks is another question. And their power comes at a significant cost in terms of resources. When figures like the aptly named Leopold Aschenbrenner – his last name means “ash burner” – call for hundreds of new power plants to power the AI future, all while we are facing calls to reduce carbon output, their vision might literally involve boiling the oceans and turning the earth to ash.

records.abstract: Our April 2023 assessment of large language models concluded that they were not ready to replace neural machine translation (NMT) despite some advantages over it (“Is Generative AI’s Translation Output Usable and for What?”). The May 2024 release of ChatGPT-4o (“o” for “omni”) reignited speculation that LLMs would displace NMT as the automated translation technology of choice. Will GPT-4o succeed in this role? Its significant new capabilities, such as incorporation of audio, video, and image processing directly into one model combined with much faster speed and lower prices led us to revisit our assessment from April 2023. In this piece, we examine ChatGPT-4o’s performance and capabilities in several areas to recommend where it should – and should not – be used as a replacement for human or neural MT.

records.abstract: It’s the end of 2023 and, rather than contemplating a bright and happy new year, many enterprise localization groups are looking at another year of austerity measures. Through most of 2023 they told us they were either holding steady on spending or cutting it. In September 38% of the global enterprises that we surveyed said there’d be no change in their spending for the next three quarters, while 39% told us they will decrease outlays over that period. As we approach the last days of 2023, we’re hearing that many of them will carry these measures into the new year. If you face similar budgetary pressures, what can you do to counter them or even convince leadership to invest more? Here’s the rub: By saving a bit on language services now, you may block substantive contributions to revenue in order to save comparatively small expenses. In this blog post, we discuss two concrete steps you can take to avoid this fate: 1) demonstrating the ROI of current localization and 2) showing the value that additional languages can bring.

records.abstract: Growth in the language sector has slowed dramatically, driven in part by increasingly capable machine translation and artificial intelligence. This shift to machine processes reflects the long-term ongoing process of digital transformation and the shift from localization as a distinct process to globalization of the entire business and its assets. This change marks the start of what CSA Research calls the “post-localization era.” In this period, the human-driven offerings of translation and localization will decline in importance in favor of a wide constellation of international content services that serve cross-functional business globalization. LSPs and enterprise language services groups that embrace this change will find that – by giving up traditional localization – they will be able to continue to grow and demonstrate strategic relevance.

records.abstract: This report describes a representative sample of commercial solutions for language management, and their suitability for companies with multimedia products. It is based on our analysis of the multimedia use case, the requirements of various stakeholders throughout the organization, and the 12 solutions’ approaches to the overall complexity of small, medium, large, and extra-large organizations language needs. This research is based on: 1) analysis of, and in-depth interviews with the providers of 12 multimedia language management solutions; 2) comprehensive interviews with 19 buyers to validate the multimedia use case; and 3) CSA Research’s extensive interactions with users of language management technology through consulting and advisory engagements at companies from small startups to global enterprises. records.title: Seven common mistakes in global websites
records.subtitle: Closing the gaps in your international customer experience
records.display_title: Seven common mistakes in global websites: Closing the gaps in your international customer experience
records.abstract: Even major enterprises can struggle to deliver a compelling international customer journey. Yet simple changes can generate large dividends in improved accessibility for multilingual content and help increase customer loyalty. This visual report provides actionable guidance to correct seven common mistakes that CSA Research frequently observes in its ongoing examination of over 3,000 major brand websites. From language selection mechanisms that baffle site visitors to incomplete journeys that leave customers befuddled and technical problems that break search engines, unresolved problems can drive (potential) customers into the outstretched arms of competitors. This report and its accompanying video (available in the attachments to the right) provide real-life examples to help you attract and retain a global audience.

We also examine the broader prospects for pluricentric languages like Spanish – that is, used in more than one country – including Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Portuguese, and Russian.

records.abstract: Selecting the right machine translation engine is a major challenge for many organizations. They worry about the quality that these systems can produce, whether they can integrate them into their technology stack, and about pricing. This report, based on a survey of 24 enterprise implementers of MT and 54 LSPs that utilize MT, reveals the concerns they face and the priorities they use in selecting engines. It also shows that specialist MT providers lead the landscape even though offerings from Big Tech companies are the most popular individual choices. With 10 figures highlighting the results, including satisfaction scores for seven popular systems in four separate areas, this report will help organizations in their quest to find the right engine to support their business needs.

This report helps Japanese brands understand the competitive landscape and value of languages for their global strategy so that they can address international markets more effectively.

records.title: Responsive machine translation
records.subtitle: How MT will evolve to deliver increasingly appropriate results
records.display_title: Responsive machine translation: How MT will evolve to deliver increasingly appropriate results
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Machine translation (MT) is on the cusp of yet another revolution as increasingly sophisticated neural engines that can adapt themselves to content and metadata will usher in the era of “responsive machine translation.” This report presents an overview of this developing technology and explains how enterprises, language service providers, and MT developers alike can prepare for it. It covers the technical components as well as the business- and content-related metadata that will enable it. The report also lays out the conditions for the next step in MT innovation – responsible machine translation – that will meet the “confidence-proof test” needed for MT to meet and exceed expectations for an ever-growing array of scenarios.

records.title: Localization analytics maturity
records.subtitle: A capability model to assess how language data enables your business
records.display_title: Localization analytics maturity: A capability model to assess how language data enables your business
records.abstract: Enterprises often struggle to define useful metrics and analytics to evaluate the international parts of their business in a form that is easily understood and digested. Businesses with very sophisticated and mature localization processes can lag significantly in their data analytics, while young startups flourish with data driving their decisions. By evaluating how organizations collect, analyze, and present localization data, we have identified six levels of localization analytics maturity: 0) inactive; 1) reactive; 2) descriptive; 3) diagnostic; 4) predictive; and 5) prescriptive. By moving from historical reporting to analytics that help shape an organization’s processes, this report shows how localization teams can enable many other functions enterprise-wide to achieve their global goals.

records.title: Dashboards for globalization success
records.subtitle: Defining metrics and analytics that help global business to succeed
records.display_title: Dashboards for globalization success: Defining metrics and analytics that help global business to succeed
records.abstract: While translation reuse analytics and process KPIs are already part of the localization team’s core deliverables, many miss out on creating business-oriented guidance that can help functions in other areas of the company interpret the degree to which local markets contribute to revenue and growth. Rarely are dashboards defined to not only report on key operational functions but also to inform and prescribe upper and C-level management decisions. As AI and machine learning with other forms of automation advance rapidly, dashboards and their underlying data will continue to evolve – just like those for automobiles. In time, much of the information that dashboards passively report today will instead automate decisions – such as what to translate, how much, and when – and other actions such as provoking a quality review or signaling an escalation. Are you ready?

records.display_title: Machine translation use at LSPs (2021): Insights on how language service providers’ use of MT is evolving
records.abstract: In the past decade machine translation has gone from something a minority of language services providers used to a basic part of their technology stack. This report, based on responses from 171 LSPs that reported using MT to a survey conducted from October 2020 through January 2021, covers nine fundamental questions about MT’s role among LSPs and how it relates to various characteristics. It emphasizes the types of MT they use and how they provision it, which types – raw or post-edited – they provide to customers, how much they use it, their quality perception, and how it affects production. These results give an up-to-date picture of how machine translation is transforming language services.

records.title: Sizing the language industry: March 2021 update
records.subtitle: The challenge of forecasting the size of a Black-Swan market
records.display_title: Sizing the language industry: March 2021 update: The challenge of forecasting the size of a Black-Swan market
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Uncertainty tied to the COVID-19 pandemic produced a roller-coaster of economic results that undermined even the most reliable statistical forecasting models. As an update to our guidance from November 2020, this report accounts for preliminary revenue reports from LSPs that have produced better than expected returns for calendar year 2020. It forecasts that the language services industry will grow faster than the overall economy in 2021. We describe the challenge of forecasting during the COVID-19 pandemic and how the industry has changed, and provide our forecast for industry growth. We then analyze how demand for language services has changed by vertical sector and examine seven factors that influence recovery. We close with recommendations for how language service providers can thrive in the face of ongoing uncertainty.

records.subtitle: How artificial intelligence drives productivity and efficiency for the language industry

records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Augmented translation is a new approach to combining the strengths of humans and machines to address growing needs for multilingual content. In contrast to traditional post-editing, which leaves translators at the end of a process and asks them to clean up garbage machine translation (MT) ouput, augmented translation places linguists at the center of a constellation of technologies that support them and extend their capabilities: enhanced translation memory, adaptive neural machine translation, automated content enrichment, next-generation terminology management, lights-out project management, and microservices-based translation management systems. The results increase the productivity and value of human linguists by providing relevant information and letting them focus on those aspects of translation that require their attention.

records.abstract: A content audit is a fundamental process for any organization wanting to improve its global customer experience. Before defining style guides, terminology, or quality processes, the company needs a good understanding of the types of content they produce and audiences that they serve. A content audit also serves to identify areas of under- and over-production of information – something that enables optimized management of product, strategical, financial, and human resource planning. While enterprises often use a content audit to assess just their websites, it is an approach that can – and should – be used across the entire global customer experience.

records.title: Regional, global, and pivot language localization
records.subtitle: Alternatives to reach markets when standard localization is not an option
records.display_title: Regional, global, and pivot language localization: Alternatives to reach markets when standard localization is not an option
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: “Full localization” into all customer languages is an ideal that few enterprises meet. Not every language offers sufficient economic reward to justify investment in traditional translation services. This report examines five alternatives to typical translation: 1) relying on third-party machine translation; 2) providing “low-grade” translation; 3) using machine translation to move between similar languages where one is a target for full localization; and 4) using other economically or 5) regionally significant languages to reach customers. It delivers guidance on which of these alternatives are likely to work for 29 major online economies. The report focuses on the language component, but does not cover payment, regulatory, cultural, and other non-linguistic localization challenges that complicate market support. It is based on results from CSA Research’s Global Revenue Forecaster™, “Can’t Read, Won’t Buy – B2B,” and “Can’t Read, Won’t Buy – B2C.”

records.title: Can’t Read, Won’t Buy – B2B
records.subtitle: Analyzing business user language preferences and behaviors in 24 countries
records.display_title: Can’t Read, Won’t Buy – B2B: Analyzing business user language preferences and behaviors in 24 countries
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Paul Daniel O'Mara, Rebecca Ray, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: Business users of high-tech products should expect just as rich a customer experience as do consumers – in their language and adapted to their market. However, many firms continue to skimp on the investment required to offer their customers a full language experience that conveys their brand, reputation, and trustworthiness at a level that makes them stand out among their competitors – especially among local and regional ones. CSA Research surveyed 956 businesspeople in 24 countries in their native languages to analyze their preferences for a localized, high-tech user experience. This report provides hard data to make the ROI case for delivering localized user interface and product content – with a focus on purchasing criteria and post-sales support. Can't Read, Won't Buy - B2B is based on an in-depth survey of 956 business users of high-tech products and services in 24 locales, conducted from November 2019 to February 2020. It is our third such survey since 2008 and is a companion report to Can't Read, Won't Buy - B2C, which was released earlier this year.

records.title: Arabic for global brands
records.subtitle: Strategies to deliver optimum customer experience in local arabic variants
records.display_title: Arabic for global brands: Strategies to deliver optimum customer experience in local arabic variants
records.abstract: Arabic poses a unique challenge for digital brands. On the one hand, it is the seventh most significant online language, representing a total audience of 222 million and an online opportunity of US$2.5 trillion in 2020. On the other hand, Arabic is not a single digital language for content marketing and customer experience. Rather, it is a mosaic of tongues derived from Classical Arabic and, in some areas, spoken alongside non-Arabic ones such as various Amazigh (aka Berber) tongues and French. In this brief, we outline regional Arabic variants for companies to evaluate, based on online audience and opportunity data from CSA Research annual benchmarks.

records.abstract: CSA Research has identified “small AI” as a differentiator in the “AI wars.” We used this term to describe the tools and applications that add value to processes and enable them to address problems that elude bigger AI applications such as machine translation (“Small AI Is Beautiful – Lots of Data Complements Buckets of Money”). Some language service providers have realized that the large amounts of clean, relevant bilingual data that courses through their client workflows can serve as the basis of improved AI-based multilingual services for their clients, many of whom struggle to find precisely this sort of training data for their internal applications (“Bridging the Multilingual Training Data Divide”). records.abstract: While language service providers often leverage machine translation (MT) for internal productivity, many of their buyers believe it is not relevant to their needs. However, recent evolution in this field is making the technology suitable for new scenarios and challenging LSPs to convert MT skeptics into adopters. This report delivers executives, sales, and marketing teams guidance on steps to be ready to sell machine translation- based services successfully to clients that worry about what it means for them. MT technology vendors will also benefit from the advice to support their service partners or when selling MT offerings themselves. This report is based on CSA Research’s studies of how the fastest growing LSPs use technology, examinations of MT deployment at LSPs and MT technology vendors, and discussions with buyers of these services.

records.abstract: As software becomes more complex and takes on critical business functions previously handled by humans, internationalization – the process of abstracting functionality away from its linguistic or cultural interface – becomes more difficult. Differences in laws, business practices, regulations, and cultural assumptions all challenge the notion that one code base can cover the entire world with just a thin layer of localization on top. Instead, developers must build complex applications with locale-specific functionality and adaptation that goes beyond traditional localization. This report describes the areas likely to create difficulty for developers and how they can respond to them effectively. This guidance is based on CSA Research’s many interactions with large technology companies that develop rich, enterprise-critical applications, and examinations of their successes and failures.

This report provides a guide to improving your cost-benefit analysis of localization.

records.title: Using MT to pivot between related languages
records.subtitle: Bridging the gap between similar languages and dialects on a budget
records.display_title: Using MT to pivot between related languages: Bridging the gap between similar languages and dialects on a budget
records.abstract: Standard translation production processes avoid the use of pivot languages – that is, translating content into one language and then retranslating from that target into others. However, using a pivot with machine translation (MT) to process dialects or related languages offers significant advantages in terms of time and cost. For languages in the same family that share a high degree of mutual intelligibility, MT can deliver high-quality results at a fraction of the cost of human translation and more efficiently than is possible by handling each target directly from the source. Thus, it provides a strategic path for localization groups to add additional locales at a low cost if they already support very similar ones. This report explains how this approach works and how to use it effectively. In this report, we describe: 1) why MT success improves with similarity between source and target; 2) how enterprises can use one locale as a pivot for MT to reach similar target languages or dialects; 3) which locale combinations are suitable. This is followed by a set of recommendations. This report is based on CSA Research’s evaluation of academic research on machine translation between similar languages and summarizes the enterprise experience in this area.

records.abstract: A narrow focus on interoperability as a matter of data formats and technology integration has led many language services organizations to miss opportunities to simplify processes and become more efficient. Ideally everything would “just work” – each action would produce the desired result and lead directly into the next step. However, inefficient processes and broken interfaces between individuals, groups, and technologies lead to waste, inconsistency, delays, and extra costs. This report presents a holistic view of interoperability – embracing people, processes, and software technologies – and how to resolve these issues. In this report, we analyze: 1) why language services organizations need a broader concept of interoperability; 2) how interoperability-related waste imposes costs on organizations and hampers their ability to act strategically; 3) how to identify and resolve interoperability problems; and 4) some of the factors that help ensure successful resolution of these issues.This report is based on CSA’s ongoing examination of interoperability and standards initiatives, discussions with language service providers about the software and process challenges they face, and consultation with enterprise buyers of language services about the difficulties they face internally and in dealing with their suppliers.

records.display_title: Four trends in intelligent content for LSPs
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Intelligent content consists of text, graphics, video, or audio materials that are self-describing, semantically rich, and interlinked. Because they encode meaning in machine-interpretable formats, computers can re-format, re-purpose, and transform them in a variety of ways and act upon them without the need for manual intervention. While enterprises face strong pressure to implement such formats because they make content more valuable, language service providers can struggle to localize such materials. This report provides background on intelligent content, discusses its benefits, and examines four changes in content production that challenge LSPs – semantic enrichment, machine-generated content, conversational content, and requirements for supporting headless devices. We analyze what language companies should expect with each of these and how they can help clients that struggle to deploy intelligent content globally. Finally, we make recommendations for how LSPs can be more efficient in dealing with this content.

records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Machine learning may be a buzzword right now, but the transformations it enables are as important as the shift to digitalization that began in the 1980s and took off with the internet. Starting in 2015, the combination of big data – amplified by ubiquitous broadband – and the powerful hardware required to run neural networks opened up innovative approaches to global content design, production, translation, and consumption. This report first defines what intelligent content is and why it matters. It then analyzes four content trends that promise to add value to the masses of information generated every second: 1) how semantically enriched content is adding knowledge to content; 2) why machine-generated material is exploding content volumes and changing the nature of text; 3) how conversational interactions are transforming content requirements and building demand for new ways to record information about users and their relationship to content; and 4) why the rise of speech-enabled and headless devices will require content intelligence. It then closes with a set of recommendations for how to prepare for the rise of intelligent content.

records.title: The bots are coming: Localizing automated agents
records.display_title: The bots are coming: Localizing automated agents
records.abstract: Chatbots – also known as online agents, interactive agents, or simply “bots” – are computer programs that interact with humans via conversation. They range from simple systems that follow decision trees for single tasks to complex personal assistants – such as Apple’s Siri or Microsoft’s Cortana – that can perform many different activities. Localizing these tools is very different from translating technical or marketing text because it requires a deeper understanding of culture and people’s conversational conventions in their own language. Chatbots pose major world-readiness challenges. Today’s development frameworks typically support only English or Chinese, so few enterprises succeed in building multilingual bots. Nevertheless, market pioneers are developing best practices for successfully deploying them. Based on in-depth interviews as part of our multilingual support knowledge base research, this report covers: the basic types of online agents; why multilingual bots complicate the localization situation; how internationalizing chatbots differs from traditional content; why transcreating them makes sense; best practices for building locale-appropriate chatbot content; and recommendations for enterprises building these tools for global use.

This TechStack provides an overview of OCR; describes its role in translation processes; discusses the past, present, and future of the technology; lists prominent OCR solutions with significant multilingual capabilities; performs a SWOT analysis; and details basic and advanced features of OCR.

records.display_title: AI is changing how LSPs manage projects

Organizations that procure language services or develop their own translation or interpreting management platforms should stay current with AI developments and determine how the latest innovations will affect them. In this report, we cover the journey from simple automation to artificial intelligence, the state of automation at LSPs based on responses to our annual global market survey, 12 steps to prepare for project management AI, and how to view AI on your projects.

records.title: TechStack: Automated content enrichment
records.display_title: TechStack: Automated content enrichment

records.abstract: Automated content enrichment (ACE) is an emerging technology that parses source and target text, creates links to relevant external resources, and can supply additional information such as terms, concepts, dates, or products. ACE makes content more intelligent for the benefit of whoever interacts with it – those who produce it, linguists, machines, or human consumers of information. It adds value at the source and in derived works such as translation. Although this technology is still in its infancy, it reflects a broader business shift toward intelligent content that can be used in many contexts and that supports knowledge-driven business activities. CSA Research expects that ACE will increasingly influence translation processes in the coming years. This report provides an overview of ACE, a discussion of why the technology matters, an examination of its history, development, and future, a SWOT analysis of current-generation offerings, a listing of translation-oriented ACE solutions, and what to look for when evaluating enrichment tools.

This report provides guidance on current and evolving demand for the language pairs participants in CSA Research’s annual Global Market Survey most frequently cited as the fastest growing or experiencing the greatest price pressure. Both buyers and suppliers of translation and interpretation services can use this data in their planning. Buyers will better understand overall market trends for language services and will learn where increasing demand for particular language pairs may result in rising prices. LSPs can use the information to better manage their supply chains and forecast expected demand from their clients and prospects.

records.title: Will AI eliminate the need for project managers?
records.display_title: Will AI eliminate the need for project managers?
records.abstract: Project management is an essential ingredient for a successful, profitable language service provider. Until recently, LSPs relied entirely on humans to oversee projects and execute individual tasks, sometimes using software to assist. Over the last few years, CSA Research has observed a growing number of language businesses based on artificial intelligence (AI) in which there are no project managers (PMs) or the few remaining ones play a modified role. In this report, we cover the journey from simple automation to artificial intelligence, the state of automation at LSPs based on responses to our annual global market survey, 12 steps to prepare for AI, and whether and when to get on the bandwagon.

records.title: Website language churn: 2016–2017
records.display_title: Website language churn: 2016–2017
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Benjamin B. Sargent
records.abstract: In any given year, global enterprises add or drop languages from their sites in response to a variety of macro-economic, business climate, and internal factors. This report examines “churn” – the likelihood that the world’s most prominent websites added or dropped any of 171 languages that CSA Research tracked across 2,648 brand sites between 2016 and 2017. This factor correlates with the stability of the economic opportunity offered by each language. High churn indicates volatile demand – that is, many enterprises dropped it in the last year. In contrast, low churn points to comparatively stable demand, reflecting a mature language market. We also include a “pick-up” rate, a measure of increasing demand. Global planners and content creators can use these two metrics to flag risks and opportunities as they decide whether to add new languages to their portfolio.

records.title: Taking the plunge: Why develop software?
records.display_title: Taking the plunge: Why develop software?
records.authors: Benjamin B. Sargent, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: The decision to develop software in-house is a difficult one for many LSPs. Although some begin early in their history, others wait until they have a more mature business before they create their first proprietary solutions. It’s a delicate balance: If they wait too long, they may miss growth opportunities, but jumping too soon can result in unfocused and wasted effort. However, by the time they reach Stage 4 in the LSP Metrix™ maturity model, our research shows that software development becomes an imperative. The need for production efficiency and service differentiation, throughout an LSP’s life cycle, are the most important triggers for the creation of bespoke systems. This report decribes three approaches to technology adoption available to LSPs, identifies the triggers that lead them to build their own systems, and discusses the stages during which different types of companies may begin development efforts. This research draws on qualitative data collected in surveys and interviews of 30 LSPs in early 2017 – as well as hundreds of surveys, briefings, and advisories conducted by CSA Research in recent years.

records.title: Benchmarking LSP websites
records.subtitle: How language companies market their activities online
records.display_title: Benchmarking LSP websites: How language companies market their activities online
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Benjamin B. Sargent
records.abstract: Your website is vital to your marketing strategies, yet delivering a compelling message that sets you apart can be tough. You may craft messages that fail to resonate with your target audience or that do not show up in search results. Understanding how other providers deliver their value proposition can help you identify strengths to promote and exploit in your online presence and weaknesses to remove. CSA Research examined 305 websites of language company service providers – including those that appear on our 2016 list of top global and regional providers. We focused our analysis on the role that websites play in business development. This report presents details about how they structure their websites and suggests ways to improve them. Marketing managers and executives will be able to benchmark their websites against competitors and find ways to improve user experience.

records.title: The winds of content are changing
records.display_title: The winds of content are changing
records.abstract: Content creation and production are undergoing fundamental change. They are moving earlier in the process of building a product or service. In some cases, the boundaries between product and content are blurring or even vanishing. Purposes and audiences are evolving. Lead times are shrinking, and source optimization that assumes long lead times and dedicated staff is disappearing. Based on CSA Research’s recent examination of how enterprises optimize their content for translation, this research piece covers: an overview of the changes that affect the landscape, five trends in content creation and production, and suggestions for how enterprises can optimize appropriately within the constraints of these rapid changes.

records.title: TechStack: Terminology management tools
records.display_title: TechStack: Terminology management tools
records.abstract: The use of terminology management tools and processes enables global enterprises and language service providers to re-purpose content and translations of small units of text. Today, no content management or localization management strategy is complete without terminology management. In this report, we explore these tools through: an overview of terminology management tools, a synopsis of their history and development, a review of key principles and features that need to be supported by the tools, a SWOT analysis, and information on types of solutions and sample applications.

records.title: Who’s who in language services and technology: 2017 rankings
records.subtitle: Ranking of global and regional providers
records.display_title: Who’s who in language services and technology: 2017 rankings: Ranking of global and regional providers
records.authors: Donald A. DePalma, Robert G. Stewart, Dr. Arle Lommel, Hélène Pielmeier
records.abstract: Tens of thousands of providers around the globe work with hundreds of thousands of professional linguists to deliver services such as translation, interpreting, and localization to organizations and individuals. This active and growing global industry accounts for US$43 in billion revenue. Language service providers (LSPs) eagerly wait for the annual release of CSA Research’s lists of top ranked companies. They rely on the rankings and results to benchmark performance against their competitors and to earn recognition among buyers of language services who otherwise may not know they exist. We have seen many buyers issue RFPs that specify they will consider only those companies ranked on these lists. To produce these rankings, CSA Research conducted its 13th consecutive study of the market for outsourced language services and technology. It is based on a comprehensive survey of industry providers. This report analyzes the market from January 2016 through June 2017.

records.title: Tech-Savvy providers nail the LSP Metrix
records.display_title: Tech-Savvy providers nail the LSP Metrix
records.authors: Benjamin B. Sargent, Dr. Arle Lommel, Hélène Pielmeier
records.abstract: Technology plays a vital role for language service providers, yet deciding how much and when to invest in language or business tools is difficult for them. Technology adoption increases as LSPs mature and is widely perceived to speed that process. However, regardless of the systems used, translation and interpreting remain largely human-delivered services. Over-aggressive spending on software introduces risk and bleeds off capital otherwise available to invest in other areas of the business. This research presents and aligns two analytical models for evaluating language service providers, LSP Metrix™ and the Tech-Savvy typology. The former is a measure of business maturity and the latter a typology based on technology adoption style.

records.title: Optimizing content for MT: A checklist
records.display_title: Optimizing content for MT: A checklist
records.abstract: Content source optimization (CSO) refers to the process of preparing text, graphics, and other content components for translation. It eliminates obstacles to efficient conversions into another language and creates material in a form suitable for multiple locales. When preparing content for machine translation (MT) processing, organizations need to be extra careful because even the best systems do not understand the text they process and usually cannot correct for even obvious errors. Careful authoring is therefore a must to deliver better MT results. This brief covers: how to determine whether MT-oriented CSO makes sense for you; basic principles for optimizing content for machine translation; how to use the checklist to evaluate your text; and how to prioritize your efforts.

records.title: Content source optimization: A checklist
records.display_title: Content source optimization: A checklist
records.abstract: Organizations that struggle to control translation costs and improve quality often find that addressing problems after they occur yields only modest gains, but when they look upstream and improve their source content, it can deliver substantial benefits throughout the content lifecycle. This brief discusses how to optimize source content to speed up the translation and localization process and reduce its cost. It addresses: the information sources we consulted; the definition of content source optimization (CSO); the benefits that the practice provides; how to use the items included in the checklist as guidance for proper CSO; instructions for using the CSA Research’s “Content Source Optimization Checklist”; and the steps you can take to deliver ongoing improvement in this area. It helps practitioners evaluate their state of optimization and suggests areas for improvement.

records.title: TechStack: Translation quality and In-Context review tools
records.display_title: TechStack: Translation quality and In-Context review tools
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Translation quality assurance and assessment (TQA) and in-context review tools assist linguists in identifying errors in translated content and fixing them. They play a vital role in helping translation providers and requesters alike understand how well translations meet expectation and what it takes to improve them. They take various approaches to identifying errors, scoring translations, and responding to errors or assessments, and include the following system types: manual error scorecards, automatic error detectors, in-context review tools, and automatic scoring systems. This brief provides: an overview of these systems, a synopsis of their history and development, a SWOT analysis of current-generation systems, information on pricing and deployment models, basic data on current and upcoming solutions, and a list of features and guidelines for implementation.

records.title: Economic opportunity by industry
records.display_title: Economic opportunity by industry
records.abstract: Managing scheduled interpreting jobs can be a daunting task for buyers of language services and their suppliers. Between April and August 2016, CSA Research investigated the state of interpreting management systems (IMSes) by conducting briefings and demos with technology vendors, and interviewing users of such systems. In this brief, we present an overview of IMSes, their evolution over time, a SWOT analysis, pricing models; and IMS solutions in the market and what to look for when selecting a system.

records.title: Does Third-Party linguistic review make sense?
records.display_title: Does Third-Party linguistic review make sense?
records.abstract: In their quest to ensure that translations meet quality expectations, some buyers of translation services work with third-party organizations to obtain linguistic reviews of content. This step is meant to assure them that content meets legal or business requirements, but comes at a cost. While CSA Research does not recommend this approach in standard workflows, we do find that third-party linguistic review does add value in specific use cases. In this brief, we: 1) define third-party review; 2) discuss the method’s pros and cons; 3) review cases where it may be required; 4) explore alternatives for cases where it is not well suited; and 5) provide implementation tips.

records.title: Account growth through client care
records.display_title: Account growth through client care
records.abstract: What is the magic that turns some buyers turn into top clients? CSA Research conducted a survey of 211 LSPs to analyze information on their top three accounts. In this brief, we examine the relationship between the size of an opportunity and the time and effort that language service providers invest in them. We offer suggestions for how to adjust sales efforts to seller’s characteristics.

records.title: Remove process waste for greater efficiency
records.display_title: Remove process waste for greater efficiency
records.abstract: Like a leaky faucet, a process that creates losses here and there can amount to a big bill at the end. However, many buyers of language services may be unaware of how subtle waste on their part contributes to quality and efficiency problems on a larger scale, even when they abide by quality management standards such as ISO 9001. In this brief, we use the principles and lessons of Japanese process management to provide guidance for enterprise translation teams that strive to achieve operational excellence to: 1) understand the basics of waste; 2) define types of waste; and 3) adopt techniques to identify and remove it.

records.title: Understanding buyer decision strategies
records.display_title: Understanding buyer decision strategies
records.abstract: When you consider expanding your sales and marketing efforts, you may find yourself hampered by a lack of knowledge about how to find profitable opportunities. If you go after particular profiles simply because they are visible, you may miss opportunities that are better for your company. If you have already zeroed in on the best opportunities, then converting them to paying customers is essential. In this brief, we focus on characteristics that will help you fine-tune your marketing efforts and outreach activities to match client and prospect needs more effectively. We examine: 1) how contract size relates to decision processes; and 2) trends toward decision-making strategies by industry. We recommend how to use these results. When combined with our research on market segmentation, these findings will help you create or fine-tune pitches that will succeed with your target segments and personas. Because they represent the best and most direct sales opportunity, we focus our attention on the authority profiles that have the most discretion in the purchasing process.

records.title: Twenty profiles of buyers of language services
records.display_title: Twenty profiles of buyers of language services
records.abstract: When language services providers try to promote the virtues of their offerings, they often comment that finding the right individual to target can amount to finding a needle in a haystack. Yet, identifying the best entry points into a prospect can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of sales and marketing efforts. Doing so combines with broader market segmentation efforts to yield more effective and targeted sales. CSA Research conducted a survey of 211 LSPs to examine information on their top three accounts. From that data we developed 20 client profiles. This brief details: five authority profiles based on the role of the contact’s within their organizations’ hierarchy; five functional profiles that focus on their business function; and 10 industry profiles that identify specific characteristics of buyers based on their industry. Use this data to understand who your likely buyers are, what they can expect from prospects, and how to identify new targets for your sales and marketing efforts.

records.title: Understanding translation quality
records.display_title: Understanding translation quality
records.abstract: Translation “quality” is notoriously difficult to define and can be a source of debate and dispute between translation providers and buyers. To give stakeholders a point of reference to explain what they mean and expect by quality, we: 1) examine different definitions of translation quality, discuss why they matter, and present a definition for translation quality that unifies these various aspects; 2) discuss how they relate to the broader field of quality management; and 3) provide recommendations for how to apply these views to improve outcomes and business relationships.

records.title: Developing the IDP market
records.subtitle: Sustainability in interpreting delivery platform offerings
records.display_title: Developing the IDP market: Sustainability in interpreting delivery platform offerings
records.abstract: Announcements of interpreting delivery platforms (IDPs) that enable remote, video, telephone, and even machine interpretation appear with ever more frequency. However, limitations restrict the adoption of many offerings. Most providers offer single-purpose applications suited for just one or two use cases and buyers have not adopted these products at the pace their developers expected. Developers and sellers must address core problems – or the IDP market will develop slowly, remain fragmented, and won’t exhibit clear leaders for quite some time. March through August 2016, CSA Research conducted 45 interviews and demos with tech vendors, users of such technologies, and interpreting experts to assess the state of interpreting technology offerings. The first report on this research, “ Interpreters at the Push of a Button,” (Aug16) presented information on selecting platforms. In this second installment, we explore IDP deployment challenges and propose solutions to sell platforms more successfully. We provide concrete advice for technology vendors, interpreting service providers that develop their own solutions, and companies that re-sell off-the-shelf products. Buy-side organizations that rely on IDPs will get a broader perspective of issues that will help them make informed decisions to help the market mature.

records.title: Digital opportunity: Under- and Over-Served languages
records.display_title: Digital opportunity: Under- and Over-Served languages
records.authors: Benjamin B. Sargent, Dr. Arle Lommel
records.abstract: Some languages historically show lower use than their market heft should warrant, such as Arabic, Hebrew, and Persian. Other languages appear more frequently than their limited market size might predict, including Bulgarian, Hungarian, and Slovak. In this brief we continue our three-year longitudinal analysis of the economic potential of online languages versus their frequency of use on the websites of prominent brands around the world. This analysis will help corporate planners focus their investment on the most necessary and lucrative languages and will guide LSPs to recommend markets that drive revenue and market share growth for their clients.

records.title: Open-Source Language-Industry ecosystems
records.display_title: Open-Source Language-Industry ecosystems
records.abstract: Where does open-source software (OSS) fit in the language sector? This brief updates our earlier analysis of six tools – GlobalSight, Moses, Okapi, OmegaT, ]project-open[, and TermWiki – and adds information on six more solutions: LanguageTool, MateCat, OpenTM2, Pootle, Serge, and translate5. It is based on phone and e-mail interviews with developers and users of open-source tools and a review of public information. We examine the range of functionality in place and explain how organizations build ecosystems of open-source tools associated with written-text translation. We do not cover either tools or infrastructure technologies for interpreters, such as WebRTC.

records.title: Fast-Growing LSPs turn to machine translation
records.display_title: Fast-Growing LSPs turn to machine translation
records.abstract: Executives at most of the LSPs we interview or survey are evaluating the role of machine translation (MT) in their businesses. They wonder where they stand compared to their peers and what competitive pressures they will face from MT and post-editing. In this brief, we examine how CEOs from 50 of the top 100 language service providers view this topic versus how those from 75 of their smaller competitors do. We discuss: 1) the importance of MT to their companies’ strategies and growth; 2) how they deal with quality challenges; 3) how they believe that it affects their buyers’ perception of human translation (HT); 4) what the effects are on translation volume, price, and demand for HT; 5) the MT-related issues that concern LSP CEOs; and 6) suggestions for how to use the insights offered by respondents.

records.title: Post-Editing goes mainstream
records.subtitle: How LSPs use MT to meet client demands
records.display_title: Post-Editing goes mainstream: How LSPs use MT to meet client demands
records.authors: Dr. Arle Lommel, Donald A. DePalma
records.abstract: Language service providers face increasing price pressure as well as growing demand from prospects and clients for post-edited machine translation (PEMT). If forces them to address the fundamental question of whether to implement MT in the workflows and how to do it. In February to April 2016, CSA Research surveyed 383 LSPs on their approach to PEMT. This report helps executives, sales staff, and production managers of LSPs of any size understand what their peers are doing with MT and what the competitive landscape looks like. The report covers: What MT is, who offers PEMT, how LSPs engage with MT, what types of content they post-edit, and changes in demand for these services. It closes with recommendations for how language companies can be more competitive with post-editing.

records.title: MT skeptics: Is the time right for Post-Editing?
records.display_title: MT skeptics: Is the time right for Post-Editing?
records.abstract: Post-editing is rapidly becoming a popular solution for content translation. Language service providers experience considerable pressure to adopt it for internal efficiency or to respond to client demands. However, CSA Research finds that about half of LSPs say they do not currently work with post-edited machine translation (PEMT). In this brief, we look at the reasons why these providers choose not to offer this service or limit their use. We then address why you need to consider adopting it and provide a decision matrix to see whether your company is a candidate for it.

records.title: Specifications improve quality and satisfaction
records.display_title: Specifications improve quality and satisfaction
records.abstract: Many translation quality disputes between enterprises and language service providers (LSPs) arise from the lack of communication and a mismatch of expertise and expectations. Formalizing project specifications improves communication, quality outcomes, and customer satisfaction. Use of common terminology and parameters can align the goals and expectations of all parties before projects begin. In this brief, we show how to apply ASTM F2575, an industry standard for translation project specifications, to address: 1) how the lack of clarity in the translation process leads to problems; 2) how the use of specifications minimizes them; 3) the issues that specifications should address; 4) how to prioritize the content of specifications; and 5) how companies can incorporate F2575’s parameters into their own processes. While this standard is by no means the only approach to developing specifications, it is representative of best practices for improving buyer-supplier interactions.

records.title: Simplifying multilingual content production with ITS 2.0
records.display_title: Simplifying multilingual content production with ITS 2.0
records.abstract: Global enterprises require efficient and cost-effective localization of XML content, but achieving this goal can be challenging due to the variety of forms XML can take. While HTML content is easier to localize, it often has its own complexities. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)’s Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) 2.0 provides a set of metadata formats that simplify working with both of these formats. As the available information about ITS requires extensive reading and synthesis, this brief summarizes: 1) the challenges of translating XML; 2) the benefits of ITS 2.0; 3) an overview of its features; and 4) a perspective on its future.
